questions.q: What row does GROUP BY CUBE (Color, Size) produce that GROUP BY ROLLUP (Color, Size) never does?
options: The grand total row
A plain detail row for each exact Color/Size combination
A subtotal by Size alone, across every Color
A subtotal by Color alone, across every Size
questions.explain: ROLLUP only rolls up right to left, so it never produces a Size-alone subtotal with Color as NULL — CUBE does, because it generates every possible combination.

questions.q: For 2 grouping columns, how many subtotal 'levels' does CUBE produce, compared to ROLLUP's 3?
options: 2 — the same as a plain GROUP BY
4 — the full power set of combinations
3 — exactly the same as ROLLUP
6 — double ROLLUP's count
questions.explain: N columns under CUBE produce 2^N combination levels; for 2 columns that's 4 (detail, Color-only, Size-only, and grand total).

questions.q: When should you reach for CUBE instead of ROLLUP?
options: Never — CUBE is deprecated in favor of ROLLUP
Only when working with date columns
When the grouping columns are independent dimensions you want to cross-tabulate every way, not a strict hierarchy
Whenever you have more than one GROUP BY column, as a default habit
questions.explain: ROLLUP fits a real hierarchy (year > quarter > month); CUBE fits independent dimensions like color and size where every combination of subtotals is meaningful.

questions.q: What does GROUPING_ID(Color, Size) let you do that calling GROUPING() on each column separately doesn't as conveniently?
options: Convert CUBE results back into a plain GROUP BY
Return the actual Color and Size values instead of NULLs
Pack the subtotal-level information into a single number, useful for filtering or ORDER BY
Remove the need for GROUP BY entirely
questions.explain: GROUPING_ID() combines multiple GROUPING() results into one number, making it easy to sort or filter rows by which subtotal level they represent.

questions.q: What is GROUPING SETS, as introduced at the end of this lesson?
options: A way to GROUP BY without using any aggregate functions
A Power BI-only feature with no T-SQL equivalent
A deprecated alias for CUBE with no real difference
A related keyword for specifying an exact custom list of subtotal combinations, instead of ROLLUP's hierarchy or CUBE's full power set
questions.explain: GROUPING SETS lets you list precisely which combinations of subtotals you want, rather than ROLLUP's fixed hierarchy or CUBE's full power set — named here, not covered as its own lesson.
